results.title: AWS cuts prices of some EC2 Nvidia GPU-accelerated instances: What changed
results.author: iTechGuides Team
highlights:
AWS reduced On-Demand prices for P4d, P4de, P5, and P5en EC2 instances by up to 45%, but the reduction is not universal. Here are the effective dates, Regions, Savings Plan changes, capacity caveats, and a practical way to calculate your real GPU savings.

...

AWS cuts prices of some EC2 Nvidia GPU-accelerated instances by up to 45%, but the June 2025 change covers only the P5, P5en, P4d, and P4de families. Lower On-Demand rates began June 1, 2025, while updated Savings Plan pricing applied to purchases after June 4. Maximum reductions apply to Amazon Linux and vary by configuration.

## Key takeaways

- AWS announced maximum On-Demand reductions of 45% for P5, 26% for P5en, and 33% for both P4d and P4de instances.
- The reduced On-Demand prices took effect June 1, 2025; Savings Plan purchases received the updated pricing after June 4, 2025.
- The headline percentages apply to Amazon Linux and can be smaller for other operating systems, Regions, instance sizes, and pricing arrangements.
- The price cut does not cover every NVIDIA-powered EC2 family, including G4dn, G5, G6, G6e, G7, G7e, or the newer P6 families.
- A cheaper GPU-hour does not automatically mean a cheaper training run, inference request, or complete AI system because storage, networking, software, idle time, and managed-service fees remain separate costs.

...

| EC2 family | NVIDIA GPU | Typical workload fit | Maximum AWS-announced reduction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P4d | A100 | Machine-learning training, inference, and HPC | Up to 33% |
| P4de | Higher-memory A100 configuration | Large-model training, inference, and HPC workloads needing more GPU memory | Up to 33% |
| P5 | H100 | Large-scale AI training and inference | Up to 45% |
| P5en | H200 | Memory-intensive AI and HPC workloads | Up to 26% |

...

AWS announced reductions of up to 45% for P5, up to 26% for P5en, and up to 33% for P4d and P4de. The qualifying phrase “up to” is important: AWS did not state that every instance size, Region, operating system, or tenancy received the maximum reduction.

AWS’s announcement does not provide a complete historical and current hourly-price table. Therefore, an exact hourly saving cannot be stated responsibly without specifying the instance size, Region, operating system, tenancy, and purchase model and then comparing the applicable AWS price records. Use the EC2 On-Demand pricing page and AWS’s Price List files or Price List API guidance for a configuration-specific calculation.

### What determines the actual discount?

- Instance size: the maximum percentage may not apply to every size in a family.
- Region: AWS pricing and availability vary by launch Region.
- Operating system: AWS says the advertised maximums apply to Amazon Linux; reductions for other operating systems are slightly smaller.
- Tenancy: shared, dedicated, and host-based arrangements can have different pricing dimensions.
- Purchase model: On-Demand, Savings Plans, and Spot use different pricing mechanisms.
- Existing commercial terms: private pricing, credits, and an existing commitment can make the effective rate different from the public list rate.

## When did the EC2 NVIDIA price cut take effect?

The reduced On-Demand pricing began on June 1, 2025. AWS published the announcement on June 5, 2025, so the announcement date was four days after the On-Demand effective date. AWS said the corresponding Savings Plan pricing applied to purchases made after June 4, 2025. The dates and scope are documented in AWS’s pricing announcement.

| Date | What happened | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| June 1, 2025 | Reduced On-Demand pricing began for the affected families. | Eligible usage from this date used the reduced On-Demand pricing, subject to the relevant configuration. |
| June 4, 2025 | Updated pricing applied to new Savings Plan purchases. | Commitment calculations made after this date should use the new applicable rates. |
| June 5, 2025 | AWS published the announcement. | This is the publication date, not the On-Demand effective date. |
| June 17, 2025 | AWS announced one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plans for P5 and P5en. | This was a later commitment-option update, separate from the original four-family price reduction. |

## Does the price cut apply in every AWS Region?

No. The price reduction concerns the affected families, but regional availability, pricing, quota, and launch capacity still have to be checked separately. AWS specifically identified new or expanded at-scale On-Demand capacity in selected Regions, not guaranteed capacity everywhere.

| Family | Regions AWS identified for at-scale On-Demand capacity |
| --- | --- |
| P4d | Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (London) |
| P4de | US East (N. Virginia) |
| P5 | Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Asia Pacific (Jakarta), and South America (São Paulo) |
| P5en | Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Asia Pacific (Jakarta) |

“At-scale On-Demand capacity” should not be read as a promise that a requested number of GPUs can always be launched. A large deployment can still encounter insufficient capacity, an EC2 quota, an Availability Zone limitation, placement-group constraints, or a lack of EFA-enabled capacity. Check the EC2 instance-by-Region documentation, request the required quotas, and test launch capacity before moving a production workload.

...

The June 2025 announcement reduced an EC2 compute line item. ... Budget for the following separately:

...

A July 2026 AWS announcement about lower EKS Auto Mode management fees is a separate change. AWS said that announcement reduced management fees for GPU and accelerated instance types beginning July 1, 2026; it was not a new reduction in EC2 instance-hour prices and should not be included in the P4d, P4de, P5, or P5en compute calculation.

...

AWS applied the reduced pricing to Savings Plan purchases made after June 4, 2025, and on June 17, 2025, AWS announced one-year EC2 Instance Savings Plans for P5 and P5en in all Regions where those families were available. AWS advertised savings of up to 40% versus On-Demand for that one-year option, but the maximum is not an automatic 40% discount for every customer or configuration.

...

## What is not included in the announced NVIDIA GPU price cut?

The June 2025 announcement was not a blanket reduction across AWS’s NVIDIA catalog. AWS’s accelerated-computing catalog includes G4dn, G5, G5g, G6, G6e, G6f, Gr6, G7, G7e, P4d, P4de, P5, P5en, and newer P6 families, along with non-NVIDIA accelerated instances. The announcement specifically covered only P4d, P4de, P5, and P5en.

G6f and Gr6f fractional-GPU configurations can be relevant when a full GPU would be wasteful; AWS lists profiles as small as one-eighth of an NVIDIA L4 GPU. Those fractional instances were not included in the June 2025 four-family price reduction. Review the AWS accelerated-computing catalog rather than assuming that a different NVIDIA-backed family received the same discount.

The P6-B200 update in the same AWS announcement should also be separated from the price cut. AWS made EC2 Instance Savings Plans available for P6-B200 instances, which had initially been offered through Capacity Blocks for ML; that was a purchasing-model change, not a stated reduction in the hourly price of P6-B200.

results.title: AWS Raised GPU Prices Twice in Six Months: What It Signals and What to Do About It - Data Storage
results.author: DataStorage Editorial Team
highlights:
| Metric | January 4, 2026 | July 1, 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Increase | ~15% | ~20% |
| Families affected | P5e, P5en (H200-based) | P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, P4de |
| Example: p5e.48xlarge | $34.61 to $39.80/hr | $39.80 to ~$47.76/hr |
| Advance notice | None, posted over a weekend | Published on AWS documentation page |

The January hike affected P5e and P5en instances specifically, the H200-based families. The July hike was broader, covering P6-B300 and P6-B200 (AWS's Blackwell-generation instances), plus P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de, essentially AWS's entire GPU reservation lineup. Older instance families saw smaller dollar increases but similar percentage jumps, meaning this wasn't a single product line getting repriced, it was the whole Capacity Blocks catalog.

The new July 1 rate card, per accelerator-hour in US regions:

| Instance Family | New Rate (per accelerator-hour) |
| --- | --- |
| P6-B300 (Blackwell) | $14.04 |
| P6-B200 (Blackwell) | $12.355 |
| P5en (US) | $6.865 |
| P5e (US) | $5.97 |
| P5 (US) | $5.191 |
| P4de (US) | $2.214 |

...

Standard on-demand and Savings Plan pricing actually moved in the opposite direction over the past year. In June 2025, AWS cut on-demand pricing for P5 instances by up to 45 percent, P5en by up to 26 percent, and P4d and P4de by up to 33 percent. That cut is still in effect for those product types.

results.title: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks Price Hike: Up 20% in 2026
results.author: Sofia Lindström
highlights:
AWS raised the hourly rates of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20% in July 2026, across six instance families (P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en and P4de), and the fourth rise of the year followed: on October 7, 2026 AWS raised the rates again, by 15% on most families, so that on eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, P6-B300 bills at $16.146 per accelerator-hour outside GovCloud, up from $14.04 in July. The scope is Capacity Blocks, which AWS’s EC2 pricing page describes as a way to reserve GPU instances in advance for ML workloads. The July start date is reported two ways: AWS notified customers on June 26 of a July 1 start (TECHi), while eCorpIT says AWS’s own revised notice moved it to July 7. eCorpIT reports that AWS says the next update is due in January 2027.

...

According to eCorpIT, AWS made the July change on its pricing page without a blog post or customer advisory: the notice and the new rates appeared on the Capacity Blocks pricing page, and the October rise took the same route. AWS’s pricing page is therefore where a change shows up. The four steps eCorpIT lists, plus the date AWS has given for the next update:

| Date | What changed | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January 3 | H200-linked rates up 15%: p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80 an hour in most regions, and from $43.26 to $49.75 in US West (N. California) | eCorpIT |
| April 1 | 10% rise on US P5, P5en and P6-B200 rates | eCorpIT |
| July | About 20% on six families; effective July 1 per the June 26 notice, July 7 per AWS’s revised notice | TECHi, eCorpIT |
| October 7 | 15% on most families, about 26.5% on P5 and P5en outside the US | eCorpIT |
| January 2027 | Next update due, as AWS states it | eCorpIT |

...

## Family by family: the October 7 rates

The table lists the October 7 rate per accelerator-hour for each family, as eCorpIT reports the schedule. eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, says AWS now lists one Capacity Block rate across regions, apart from GovCloud on P6, and puts P5 at $5.970 per accelerator-hour in all listed regions. AWS’s own Capacity Blocks pricing page also lists P4d, which is not among the six July families, at $1.696 per accelerator-hour for standard AWS regions, the cheapest Nvidia family on that schedule.

| Family | October 7 rate per accelerator-hour | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | $16.146 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $14.04 in July |
| P6-B200 | $14.208 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $12.355 in July |
| P5 | $5.970 | All listed regions, per eCorpIT; up 15% from $5.191 in US regions and about 26.5% from $4.72 outside the US, July rates |
| P5e | $6.866 | Up 15% from $5.97 in July; used in the p5e.48xlarge series below |
| P5en | $7.895 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $6.865 in US regions and about 26.5% from $6.241 elsewhere, July rates |
| P4de | $2.546 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $2.214 in US regions in July |
| P4d | $1.696 | Standard AWS regions, from AWS’s Capacity Blocks pricing page |

...

Rank.ai’s November 10, 2026 snapshot lists on-demand p5.48xlarge at $55.04 an hour in us-east-1, or $6.88 per GPU-hour. A Capacity Block at the October 7 P5 rate of $5.970 per accelerator-hour is $47.76 an hour, 13% below that list price. On-demand P5 pricing was also cut earlier: as of November 13, 2026, AWS’s June 5, 2025 announcement says the P5 reduction of up to 45% applied to On-Demand pricing from June 1, 2025 and to Savings Plan purchases after June 4, 2025.

...

With blocks bookable up to 8 weeks ahead, a block bought before the January 2027 update can start weeks later at the old rate. AWS gives only “January 2027”

results.title: AWS GPU Price Increases 2026: What to Do About It
results.author: Kiril Urbonas
highlights:
AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block prices for ML in January and again on 1 July 2026, so re-run your GPU budget now. Measure utilization per block, split training from inference, price the portable training half at specialist clouds, and renew only blocks you keep above roughly 70% busy. Production inference inside AWS usually stays put.

...

## The rates as of October 2026

These are the per-accelerator-hour Capacity Block rates on AWS's pricing page at the end of October 2026. Every instance has 8 accelerators, so multiply by 8 for the instance-hour.

| Instance | Accelerator | Region shown | Per accelerator-hour | Per instance-hour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | 8 x B300 | US East (N. Virginia) | $16.146 | $129.17 |
| P6-B200 | 8 x B200 | US East (N. Virginia) | $14.208 | $113.66 |
| P5en | 8 x H200 | US East (N. Virginia) | $7.895 | $63.16 |
| P5e | 8 x H200 | US East (Ohio) | $6.866 | $54.93 |
| P5 | 8 x H100 | US East (N. Virginia) | $5.970 | $47.76 |
| P4de | 8 x A100 | US East (N. Virginia) | $2.546 | $20.37 |

When we first wrote this in September, P6-B300 was about $14.04 and P6-B200 about $12.355, so the published rates have moved up roughly another 15% since. The page says prices are updated regularly based on supply and demand, that the next scheduled update is January 2027, and that you pay the rate in effect when you buy, even if the block starts after an update. That last point is the one to act on: if you know you need a block in Q1, buying it before January locks today's rate.

...

As of October 2026, a P5 Capacity Block (8 x H100) lists at $5.970 per accelerator-hour in US East (N. Virginia), about $47.76 per instance-hour. H200-based P5en is $7.895, and Blackwell P6-B200 is $14.208. You pay the rate in effect when you purchase, and AWS's next scheduled price update is January 2027.

results.title: Medium
results.author: allglenn
highlights:
On June 26, 2026, AWS updated its published Capacity Blocks pricing page with new per-accelerator hourly rates effective July 1, roughly a 20% increase across every major instance family. Reporting that cross-referenced AWS’s own documentation puts the new US-region rates at: the P6-B300 billed at $14.04, the P6-B200 at $12.355, the P5 (US regions) at $5.191, the P5 (non-US) at $4.72, the P5e at $5.97, the P5en (US) at $6.865, the P5en (non-US) at $6.241, and the P4de (US) at $2.214 per accelerator-hour. AWS’s stated rationale, repeated verbatim from the January adjustment, is that “EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing vary based on supply and demand patterns… This price adjustment reflects the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter.”

...

That framing deserves scrutiny, because July wasn’t the first move this year. On January 4, 2026, AWS raised Capacity Block prices roughly 15%, and it did so, as InfoQ documented, with $34.608/hr becoming $39.799/hr uniformly across every region for the p5e.48xlarge instance. Cloud economist Corey Quinn’s read on that first move, cited by InfoQ, was blunt: “This was AWS updating the published base rates on their pricing page… That’s a policy decision, not supply/demand.”

results.title: AWS hikes prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks: What changed
results.author: iTechGuides Team
highlights:
AWS hikes prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks amid soaring GPU demand, but the change is not a blanket EC2 GPU price increase. AWS reportedly raised selected Capacity Block reservation rates by about 15% in January 2026 and about 20% from July 1, 2026. Capacity Blocks are prepaid reservations for scheduled, scarce accelerator capacity.

The distinction matters for cloud architects and FinOps teams. Standard On-Demand and Savings Plans pricing was not included in the reported increases, while customers buying future H100, H200, Blackwell, or other supported accelerator capacity may now pay more for predictable cluster access.

...

## Key takeaways

- AWS reportedly increased selected EC2 Capacity Block rates by approximately 15% on January 6, 2026, then approximately 20% more for selected offerings effective July 1, 2026.
- Capacity Blocks are prepaid reservations for specified accelerator capacity, not ordinary hourly EC2 pricing; the reservation price is fixed after purchase, according to AWS billing documentation.
- The reported increases affect selected Capacity Block reservation rates for families including P5, P5e, P5en, P4de, P6-B200, and P6-B300, rather than all AWS GPU instances.
- Capacity Blocks can be rational for deadline-sensitive training or inference, but prepaid underutilized time, separate operating-system charges, and the absence of Savings Plan or Reserved Instance discounts can make them expensive.
- On-Demand, Spot, Savings Plans, Trainium, other hyperscalers, and specialist GPU clouds are alternatives, but each trades away some combination of availability, portability, software compatibility, or operational simplicity.

## What changed in AWS EC2 Capacity Block pricing?

AWS changed the price of selected EC2 Capacity Block reservations twice in 2026, according to separate reports. The January event primarily concerned selected P5 offerings, while the July report covered a broader group of Capacity Block reservation rates. These reports should not be summarized as a single increase across all EC2 GPU capacity.

| Date | Reported change | Scope | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| January 6, 2026 | Approximately 15% | Selected Capacity Blocks, particularly P5/H200-related capacity | It was not a blanket increase to all EC2 GPU On-Demand or Savings Plan rates |
| July 1, 2026 | Approximately 20% | Selected Capacity Block reservation rates, including P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de offerings | It does not mean every instance family or every AWS region received the same increase |

Network World reported the January 6 increase and said AWS attributed the adjustment to expected supply-and-demand patterns. A later Investing.com report carried by Yahoo Finance described an approximately 20% increase effective July 1 for selected reservation rates.

Capacity Block prices are dynamic, so a live quote can differ by instance type, region, start date, duration, and available supply. Check the current AWS Capacity Block pricing page immediately before committing to a reservation.

...

## What Capacity Block rates were reported in 2026?

The January examples below are effective hourly rates reported for the entire Capacity Block instance, not ordinary EC2 On-Demand prices. The July figures were reported as hourly rates per accelerator, so they cannot be compared directly with the January instance-level examples without accounting for accelerator count and the complete instance configuration.

| Reported event | Offering | Region or scope | Before | After or reported rate | Unit qualification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| January 6, 2026 | p5e.48xlarge | US East (Ohio) | $34.608/hour | $39.799/hour | Effective hourly rate for the Capacity Block instance |
| January 6, 2026 | p5en.48xlarge | US East (Ohio) | $36.184/hour | $41.612/hour | Effective hourly rate for the Capacity Block instance |
| January 6, 2026 | p5e.48xlarge | US West (N. California) | $43.26/hour | $49.749/hour | Effective hourly rate for the Capacity Block instance |
| January 6, 2026 | p5en.48xlarge | US West (N. California) | $45.23/hour | $52.015/hour | Effective hourly rate for the Capacity Block instance |
| July 1, 2026 | P6-B300 | Reported offering | Not stated | $14.040/hour | Reported hourly rate per accelerator |
| July 1, 2026 | P6-B200 | Reported offering | Not stated | $12.355/hour | Reported hourly rate per accelerator |
| July 1, 2026 | P5 | US regions | Not stated | $5.191/hour | Reported hourly rate per accelerator |
| July 1, 2026 | P5 | Non-US regions | Not stated | $4.720/hour | Reported hourly rate per accelerator |
| July 1, 2026 | P5e | Reported offering | Not stated | $5.970/hour | Reported hourly rate per accelerator |
| July 1, 2026 | P5en | US regions | Not stated | $6.865/hour | Reported hourly rate per accelerator |
| July 1, 2026 | P5en | Non-US regions | Not stated | $6.241/hour | Reported hourly rate per accelerator |
| July 1, 2026 | P4de | US regions | Not stated | $2.214/hour | Reported hourly rate per accelerator |

The reported figures require careful interpretation. A per-accelerator rate is not the total host price, total block price, or total training-run price. P5e and P5en configurations can differ in networking, memory, and platform characteristics, while region and operating-system charges can change the invoice. AWS’s live offering returned during the reservation search is the authoritative price for a specific purchase.

...

AWS announced in June 2025 that it had reduced On-Demand pricing for selected P4, P4de, P5, and P5en instances by as much as 45%, depending on family and platform. AWS also made certain P6-B200 instances eligible for Savings Plans after initially offering them through Capacity Blocks only. The AWS pricing announcement documents that separate change.

results.title: Two AWS GPU Price Hikes in Six Months: Rethinking Your AI Compute Mix - Upendra Sengar Blog
results.author: Upendra Sengar
highlights: In early July, AWS raised EC2 Capacity Block prices 20% across its main GPU instance families. That is the second hike in six months, following a 15% increase on January 4. If you are on H100-based P5 instances, you are now paying $5.19 per GPU hour. B300 slots hit $14.04 per GPU hour. For a team running a p5e.48xlarge continuously, the January hike alone pushed the bill from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour. The July hike adds another layer on top of that.

results.title: The bill is increasing even though prices haven't been raised | What is actually happening with AWS, Azure, and GCP｜梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
results.author: 梟 〜GLEANINGS〜
highlights:
I checked the AWS pricing page and What's New, Microsoft's licensing notices and Partner Center announcements, and the Google Cloud pricing change notification page. I went through them all, and as of September 2, 2026, there is no official announcement that base prices for general-purpose compute and storage are being raised across the board.

In response to an inquiry from DatacenterDynamics, AWS replied, “AWS's commitment to not raise pricing on fixed pricing models like On Demand and Savings Plans remains unchanged.”

...

### AWS GPU reservation slots have already gone up twice

However, it is not the case that there are no price increases at all.

AWS has a menu called EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, which allows you to reserve GPU computing resources for a set period. This pricing page states the following:

“Reservation prices are updated regularly based on trends in supply and demand for EC2 Capacity Blocks. The current prices are scheduled to be updated next in October, 2026.”

They are updated regularly based on supply and demand, with the next revision scheduled for October 2026. In other words, this menu is designed with the premise that prices will fluctuate.

In fact, it has moved twice since the beginning of 2026. In January, the p5e.48xlarge equipped with NVIDIA H200 was revised from $34.61 to $39.80 per hour in most regions, and the p5en.48xlarge was revised from $36.18 to $41.61. In July, after initially being announced for July 1 and then changed to July 7, the revisions covered P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de. The P6-B300 is at a level of $14.04 per hour per accelerator.

The prices for January mentioned here are only the amounts after the revision as of January. Because it went up again in July, the p5e.48xlarge currently on the pricing page is $47.76 per hour. That is exactly a 20 percent increase from $39.80.

AWS does not publish these revision rates. Since they do not keep old prices, the figures of “15 percent” and “20 percent” are calculated by news organizations and technical blogs that kept records of the price lists before and after the revisions. They are simply separate calculation results lined up, such as the January revision being exactly 15 percent and the July P5 revision being exactly 20 percent. It is not that AWS said “we are raising prices by 15 to 20 percent,” and the new and old prices themselves mentioned above are also based on the records of the reporting side.

And one more point. There are no individual notifications for these revisions in AWS's What's New or on their blog. What exists is the fact that the pricing page has been rewritten and the next scheduled update notice appearing in small print on that page. Price increases are being carried out in a way that you cannot notice unless you go looking for them.
